ST. LOUIS — Rep. Wesley Bell defeated former Rep. Cori Bush in a Democratic primary rematch, NBC News projects, in the latest chapter of a long-term fight over a deep-blue St. Louis-based district.
Bell overwhelmed Bush on the airwaves, fending off her push to make the race a referendum on his support for U.S. aid to Israel.
In total, Bell’s campaign and outside allies outspent Bush by a staggering 27-to-1 ratio, according to AdImpact, an ad-tracking service. United Democracy Project — the super PAC linked to the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, the pro-Israel advocacy group known as AIPAC — spent $2 million to support Bell, largely through negative ads attacking Bush. One such ad slammed Bush for being critical of former Vice President Kamala Harris.
It was a reference to Bush’s criticizing the Biden-Harris administration for supporting Israel amid what she deemed a genocide in Gaza. She endorsed Harris in the 2024 election.
As Bell cast his vote Tuesday, he criticized Bush for focusing on Israel and talking “over and over … about an issue that is not impacting folks right here in St. Louis.”
“And while we take those issues seriously, you know, the M in Missouri doesn’t stand for Middle East,” Bell told NBC News. “It stands for Missouri.”
At a campaign stop later Tuesday, Bush hit back at Bell’s claims and said Missourians “are not happy” that he filled his “campaign coffers” with money from outside groups.
“Why are they meddling in our primaries?” she asked. “Why does he allow that?”
AIPAC loomed large in the race after it helped Bell oust Bush two years ago. United Democracy Project poured $9.3 million into ads in that primary, according to AdImpact, accounting for nearly half of the spending in the race.
Sidney Clark, a Democratic candidate for state representative currently serving in local government, said he supported Bell in 2024 but was voting for Bush this cycle because Bell, in his view, has “been paid for.”
“There are people out there who are using their money and financial influence to buy candidates, and I think that’s the wrong direction for our country,” Clark said after having voted at a St. Louis polling place.
Airest Wilson, another Democratic voter, told NBC News that candidates who take corporate money cross a red line for him — even if they are otherwise aligned with his political views.
“They don’t get that money for free,” he said. “You got to represent their interests. You can’t represent the constituents freely.”
“Cori, it took a lot of courage, but she rejected dark money. So that’s why I support Cori,” Wilson added.
This year, Bush ran two TV ads in the primary, each touching on multiple issues. But both linked Bell to AIPAC and cast him as more interested in sending money to Israel than Missourians, including those suffering from the aftermath of last year’s tornado.
Bell presented himself as a fighter against President Donald Trump, saying of Bush in one of his ads: “She fights Kamala Harris, Joe Biden and other Democrats.”
Bush said Tuesday that if she were to lose, it would not be a setback for the progressive movement.
“If there is a loss, then that just means that there is more work for us to do,” she said.
Asked whether she could see herself voting for Bell if he wins the primary, Bush told NBC News: “See myself voting for a Republican? Oh, I don’t think that’s on the ballot for me.”

The results were in before U.S. Rep. Wesley Bell’s election night watch party could even get into swing.
When the Associated Press called the race for Bell over former Congresswoman Cori Bush around 8 p.m., people were still very much filtering in and the music hadn’t even started.
Get a fresh take on the day’s top news
Subscribe to the St. Louis Daily newsletter for a smart, succinct guide to local news from award-winning journalists Sarah Fenske and Ryan Krull.
The atmosphere at the Marriott Grand Hotel was slightly less kinetic than two years ago, which perhaps makes sense for an incumbent winning reelection rather than a candidate ousting a sitting congresswoman. (The room was also smaller.)
Still, there were plenty of Bell supporters on hand—some who went way back.
Over a decade ago, Marie Dubb, who now owns her own transportation company, worked for the business school at Florissant Valley Community College. At the time, Bell was an adjunct professor in the criminology and criminal justice program.
Dubb says it has been “absolutely phenomenal” watching him go from adjunct to department chair to St. Louis County prosecutor to congressman. Dubb showed up to his campaign watch party wearing a pair of American flags on her head. She described Bell as a “genuine and studious person. He does exactly what he says he says he’s going to do. “
The first batch of results—representing 16 percent of the total vote—came in around 7:30 p.m. The results were in Bell’s favor by a margin of four to one. Not long after that, before few other totals had been publicly posted, the AP called the race for Bush.
The contest was a rematch from two years ago, when Bell bested Bush by five points, 51 to 46.
As was the case last cycle, the most talked about difference between the two candidates was their stance on Israel. Bush called for ending U.S. military aid to Israel. Bell, while critical of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, maintained that the U.S. should support its allies, including Israel. The pro-Israel lobbying group AIPAC this cycle spent roughly $2.5 million opposing Bush through its United Democracy Project. Another outside group backing centrist Democrats, New Democrat Majority PAC, spent about $1.1 million supporting Bell. That was significantly less money than two years ago, when AIPAC’s generosity toward Bell made it the most expensive primary in congressional history (a record it did not hold for long).
While foreign policy got the most oxygen, it was hardly the only thing on voters’ minds. Bush blasted Bell for failing to secure more federal disaster aid following the May 16 tornado. The force of that argument, however, was undercut by reporting that showed Bush had raised money off tornado relief efforts. Some of that money flowed to a PAC that paid salaries to both Bush and her husband, Cortney Merritts. Merritts also faced criminal charges related to alleged pandemic loan fraud. The case ultimately ended in a hung jury, but the cumulative effect of the controversies reinforced the idea that Bush “has her own agenda,” as Bell’s campaign argued in its advertising. Bell’s messaging also tied those allegations of Bush and her husband lining their own pockets to the broader theme of self-dealing that has become a defining characteristic of the second Donald Trump presidency—and hit Bush hard for a TV interview in which she suggested she wasn’t sure she could endorse Kamala Harris (once Biden stepped down, she swiftly did).
The reports of Bush’s fundraising off of tornado relief struck a particular chord with Justin Idleburg, who was on hand at Bell’s watch party. He lives in a tornado-impacted area. “That made me feel some kind of way,” he said. He also didn’t buy into the notion that Bell’s outside funding was an issue. It’s politics, what do you expect? He was in for Bell, though he predicted his margin of victory would be less than last time around.
Bell also had ample resources to put his message in front of voters, outraising and outspending Bush by a wide margin. Over the previous year and a half, he raised roughly $3.6 million, about three times Bush’s total, and that was before accounting for the millions of dollars spent by outside groups on his behalf.
Heading into tonight’s race, political observers wondered whether the outsider fervor on the progressive wing of the Democratic Party—the same energy that helped elect New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani—would also be on display in St. Louis. It clearly wasn’t. That was likely due in part to the fact that Bush was no longer as convincing of an anti-establishment figure after serving two terms in Congress. In many ways, this contest resembled two incumbents squaring off against one another.
Bell must now beat the Republican nominee in November, which is generally a formality in the staunchly Democratic district. Republicans Andrew Jones and Paul Berry III were vying for the Republican nomination.
Despite the contentious race, Bush and Bell have a number of issues on which they agree. Both have called for dismantling the federal Immigration and Customs Enforcement Agency. Bell specifically said the agency should be “stripped for parts.”
At Bell’s watch party, Chris Luckett, who also knew Bell back in his Flo Valley days, walked in a few minutes after the race’s early call. He wasn’t surprised.
“I was nervous for him in the last two weeks,” he said. “But I told everyone it was going to be a landslide.”
